Article Title: UPI charges: Lok Sabha passes bill for government to make changes
Article Text:
The FM said the charge will apply to merchants and not to users and will help banks and fintech invest in infrastructure and innovation

NEW DELHI: The Lok Sabha on Thursday passed a Bill that seeks to ease tax rules to attract investments and remove the existing legal provision that prevents banks and payment service providers from charging Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on notified electronic payment modes.The Bill — passed without discussion amid din — also proposes to remove the linkage between the Payment and Settlement Systems Act and the I-Tax Act and give legal backing to the government to modify the zero-MDR framework on UPI and RuPay card transactions. Outside the House, however, there was an exchange between FM Nirmala Sitharaman and Congress MP Jairam Ramesh. Ramesh said the Bill opens the doors for MDR. The FM responded, saying the charge will apply to merchants and not to users and will help banks and fintech invest in infrastructure and innovation.“More importantly, the UPI and services steering committee headed by NPCI is yet to decide on the MDR. This will happen after Parliament passes the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026... All this could have been discussed on the floor of the House if your party @INCIndia (Congress) engages constructively in Parliament when the Bill was/is tabled,” she said.While leaving person-to-payments outside MDR’s ambit, banks and fintechs may be permitted to charge 0.25% to 0.4% on payments to businesses in excess of Rs 2,000 with an overall ceiling on how much can be charged.Officials have argued that the levy will be lower than what is charged on credit and debit cards, and most merchants will not pass it on to consumers.
Article Summary: The bill also proposes to remove the linkage between the payment and settlement systems act and the i-tax act. Outside the house, there was an exchange between fm nirmala sitharaman and congress mp jairam ramesh. The fm said the charge will apply to merchants and not to users.

Article Title: Government spending on education below Unesco's 15% standard
Article Text:
The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India remains just above Unesco's minimum GDP benchmark for education, but the sector's share in government spending has slipped below the prescribed threshold. Education accounts for 4.1% of GDP but 14.2% of total public expenditure, down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, Unesco's 2026 SDG 4 scorecard has shown.The funding picture assumes significance because India continues to lag on secondary school completion. Its latest lower secondary (Classes VI-VIII) completion rate is 86% as against its 99% national benchmark for 2025, while upper secondary (Classes IX-XII) completion rate is 51% as against 84%. Unesco classifies progress at both levels as slow.Under the Education 2030 framework, countries committed to spending 4-6% of GDP and/or 15-20% of public expenditure on education. The scorecard uses the lower thresholds as minimum benchmarks. India meets one. Its spending on education has remained at 4.1% of GDP since 2015, but its share of public expenditure has declined 1.5 percentage points to 14.2%.Among major emerging economies, China too meets one benchmark, at 4% of GDP (11.9% of public spending), while figures for Brazil are 5.6% and 12.9%. South Africa meets both, at 6% and 19.1%, while Indonesia, Bangladesh and Pakistan meet neither.The pattern is common among developed economies too: the US, UK, Germany and France meet the GDP threshold but not the public expenditure benchmark, while Sweden and Switzerland meet both.Unesco noted that richer countries tend to meet the GDP benchmark but not the public expenditure threshold because they raise more revenue, while education often accounts for a larger share of budgets in poorer countries.Latest data show 39 of 205 countries, or 19%, meeting both benchmarks, while 72, or 35%, meet neither. Another 64 countries, including India, spend above 4% of GDP but below 15% of public expenditure. Among high-income countries, 11% meet both benchmarks and 50% follow India's pattern.India, however, has larger unmet schooling needs. Lower secondary completion has risen from 81% in 2015 to 86% but remains 13 percentage points below its 99% benchmark. Even Unesco's "feasible" 2025 benchmark of 90% is four points above the latest rate.This is despite programmes operating at scale. Unesco's India profile says Samagra Shiksha supports about 15.6 crore learners, while PM-Poshan covers around 11.8 crore children in 11.2 lakh government and aided schools. The trend is part of a broader global concern. The scorecard concludes that, on average, countries are "moving away" from the public education expenditure benchmarks of at least 4% of GDP or 15% of total public expenditure.
Article Summary: Education accounts for 4.1% of gdp but 14.2% of total public expenditure. This is down from 15.7% in 2015 and below the 15% benchmark, unesco says. The funding picture assumes significance because india continues to lag on secondary school completion.

SRINAGAR: The Forum for Human Rights in J&K has called for full restoration of statehood and repeal of 2019 Reorganisation Act, cautioning that linking statehood to the security situation and terrorist attacks could erode democratic rights in the Union territory.It presented its annual report “Seven Years Under Union Rule — With a Special Section on Ladakh & Pakistan-held Territories of J&K (Aug 2025–July 2026)” to National Conference president Farooq Abdullah, PDP president and former J&K CM Mehbooba Mufti, CPM’s MY Tarigami and Congress’s J&K president Tariq Hamid Karra.The forum said arguments that restoration of statehood is “not appropriate” because of security concerns and terrorist attacks are dangerous and could be used to undermine people’s democratic rights.It also backed statehood for Ladakh and its inclusion in the Sixth Schedule of the Constitution.It praised J&K HC for a series of orders quashing detentions under Public Safety Act and granting bail under UAPA and PSA “…but we are constrained to note that its repeated strictures do not appear to have led to course correction by police,” the report said.The forum, an informal group of concerned citizens, is co-chaired by former Union home secretary Gopal Pillai and Radha Kumar, a former member of the group of interlocutors for J&K. The report also alleged a familiar backlash against Kashmiris after terrorist attacks, including the recent Red Fort blast in New Delhi, saying they faced housing discrimination, forced evictions, aggressive verification and hostility from neighbours, shopkeepers, and co-workers.
Article Summary: The forum also backed statehood for ladakh and its inclusion in the sixth schedule of the constitution. Article Title: Two memorials of 1962 war heroes figure in 27 places formally named in Arunachal
Article Text:
Havildar Shere Thapa of the 2nd Battalion, Jammu & Kashmir Rifles, was credited with saving the Subansiri Valley during the 1962 Chinese aggression

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, set up in memory of 1962 China war hero Havildar Shere Thapa, is one of the 27 places in Arunachal that the Union government on Friday formally named by their standard names on the official Indian map.Havildar Shere Thapa of the 2nd Battalion, Jammu & Kashmir Rifles, was credited with saving the Subansiri Valley during the 1962 Chinese aggression. He was part of a team to delay the advance of the enemy. On Nov 18, 1962, undaunted by the advance of the Chinese troops, he continued to engage the enemy from his position despite his buddy succumbing to enemy action. The Chinese suffered heavy losses, and their advance was delayed by 72 hours. The Indian Army installed a memorial in his name.Another name, Jaswant Garh, which houses the memorial of Indian martyr Rifleman Jaswant Singh Rawat on Tawang Road, also figured in the list. Located at 10,000 feet on the highway to Tawang, it marks the site where he single-handedly fought Chinese forces for 72 hours during the 1962 war. The memorial has been built in honour of his extraordinary bravery at the Battle of Nuranang.Jairampur, an important logistics hub in Changlang district which is known as the gateway to the eastern border region supporting movements of security forces towards eastern Arunachal and the Myanmar frontier, also figures in the list.One of the most strategically important high-altitude passes, Thag La, where one of the opening battles between Indian and Chinese forces took place in 1962, has also been formally identified. The list also includes Bisa village and strategically important high-altitude mountain passes in the region: Dzo La, Riza La and Pukur La.By formally naming some of the places, famous for the memorials of the Army war heroes, the government is paying homage to bravehearts who laid down their lives fighting for India in the northeastern state.
Article Summary: Havildar shere thapa of the 2nd battalion, jammu & kashmir rifles, was credited with saving the subansiri valley during the 1962 chinese aggression. Sher-e-thapa memorial is one of the 27 places in arunachal that the union government on friday formally named by their standard names.

Article Title: 'Dard, data, daulat': Rahul Gandhi targets Centre over unemployment at ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event
Article Text:
Rahul Gandhi addresses the gathering during the 'Chhatron Ki Goonj' program, in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh.

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday described India’s youth as the country’s biggest strength, but said a lack of jobs, expensive education, paper leaks, poor access to credit and the growing use of AI were holding them back.Speaking at the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ programme at KP Ground in Prayagraj, Rahul told the gathering, “You are power and pride of India; when I say this, I talk about every Indian citizen.” He said he wanted to speak about “dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)”, framing his address around the problems facing young Indians and the economic resources he believes should belong to them.Rahul said India’s nearly 40 crore young people were its “greatest strength”, adding that while there was much discussion about America, China and Russia, “India’s youth [are] unparalleled.” He argued that the country's future would depend on the potential of its young population and the data they generate.He said artificial intelligence was also built on people’s data and argued that this data should be treated as an asset belonging to Indians. Rahul criticised the growing use of AI in discussions about employment, saying technological changes could further threaten jobs unless young people benefited from the economy being built around their data.Rahul also spoke about his connection to Prayagraj, describing the city as his family’s home and recalling its past as an important educational centre. He said Allahabad University had once been among the country's best universities.Rahul said young Indians were being trapped in a “chakravyuh”, with education becoming increasingly expensive while degrees often failed to translate into jobs.“Today, education certificates have no meaning in India because they cannot give you job,” he said, arguing that students could spend years and large amounts of money on education without finding meaningful employment.Rahul said the problems extended across several routes into the workforce. “All doors of employment are closed in India,” he said, pointing to a decline in manufacturing, difficulties in securing loans, government-exam paper leaks and AI-driven job losses.“Decline in manufacturing, hard-to-come-by loans, paper leaks, AI replacing jobs – all this is hurting India's youth,” Rahul said.He blamed demonetisation and GST for hurting small industries, alleged that banks were failing to provide adequate credit to small and medium businesses, and criticised the privatisation of public-sector companies. He also argued that AI could further reduce corporate employment while young Indians were increasingly pushed towards gig work.Rahul framed these problems as part of what he called the broader “system”, arguing that economic and political power had become concentrated among a small number of people. He linked this to his criticism of large corporations, the government and the RSS, alleging that they exercised disproportionate influence over India's institutions.Rahul said recent student protests showed that young Indians were beginning to challenge the system. “Youths lit a light in darkness, and in doing so, changed the country,” he said.He urged young people to confront their fears without resorting to hatred or violence. “You cannot hate or be violent,” Rahul said, adding, “We will never resort to hatred or violence; will change the system with love and affection.”
Article Summary: Rahul gandhi spoke at the 'chhatron ki goonj' programme in prayagraj, uttar pradesh. He said he wanted to speak about ‘dard (pain), data, and daulat (wealth)’ he argued that the country's future would depend on its young population.

Article Title: India to recover 'Green Boots' climber's body from Everest after 30 years: Report
Article Text:
"Green Boots," the climber India is bringing home. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

The climber behind the ‘ Green Boots ’ mystery

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The body of an Indian climber believed to have become the mountaineering world’s infamous “Green Boots” could finally be brought down from Mount Everest, three decades after he died while descending from the summit.India is preparing a high-altitude recovery mission to retrieve the remains of Dorje Morup, an Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) personnel who died on Mount Everest in 1996, according to a detailed report by the BBC.Morup’s body has remained frozen at about 8,500 metres on the northern side of Everest for nearly 30 years. The remains became known among climbers as “Green Boots” because of the distinctive bright green mountaineering boots visible on the body.The ITBP is now looking for a specialist team capable of undertaking the difficult recovery operation. The force hopes to bring the remains back to India by September, after which DNA testing would be carried out to establish Morup’s identity conclusively, the BBC reported.If the identification is confirmed, his remains will be returned to his family in Ladakh.Morup was 48 when he joined a six-member ITBP expedition that attempted to climb Everest from the Chinese side in 1996.The expedition was seeking to become the first Indian team to reach the summit from that route.Three members of the expedition eventually turned back because of a snowstorm, while Morup and fellow climbers Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor continued towards the summit.All three reached the top, but disaster struck as they attempted to descend.A blizzard hit the mountain and killed the three climbers. Their bodies were left on Everest, as recovering bodies from the mountain is itself an extremely dangerous undertaking.For years, the body now known as “Green Boots” was assumed to belong to Paljor. However, surviving members of the 1996 expedition, along with information about the climbers’ final radio communications and the location of the body, have led authorities to believe that it was actually Morup.An ITBP official told BBC that Morup’s clothing and climbing equipment had also helped authorities identify the remains in recent years.The body has since become one of the most recognisable markers on the route to Everest’s summit, passed by climbers making their way through the mountain’s notorious “death zone”.For Morup’s family in Ladakh, the operation could finally resolve a mystery that has lasted three decades.His wife, Konchak Yangskit, told the BBC that she struggled to accept his death because she had never seen his body.Morup had told her before leaving for the expedition that he would return home after making the country proud. He had also asked her to look after their children and come to the airport to receive him when he returned.His son, Punchok Dorjai, told the BBC that the family plans to hold a funeral near Martyrs Park in Leh if the remains are confirmed as his.He also said the family intends to keep the green boots that gave Morup's remains their enduring identity on Everest.
Article Summary: Dorje morup died on mount everest in 1996. His body has remained frozen at about 8,500 metres on the northern side of everest for nearly 30 years. The remains became known among climbers as ‘green boots’ because of the distinctive bright green mountaineering boots visible on the body.

Article Title: 'Army safeguarding territory': Arunachal CM Pema Khandu rejects Chinese encroachment
Article Text:
Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu on Saturday rejected reports of Chinese military encroachment in the state and said that the Army was effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory.Speaking to reporters, Khandu said, "No signs of encroachment in Arunachal Pradesh; Indian Army effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory."Khandu's remarks came a day after the Centre identified 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh by their standard names on the official map of the country, amid China's repeated attempts to rename places in the border state.The government said the exercise was aimed at ensuring the correct identification of the locations and improving public awareness of their geographical and historical significance."Identifying them formally on the Survey of India map of Arunachal Pradesh is aimed at facilitating their accurate recognition and better awareness among the public at large," an official statement said.New Delhi has consistently rejected Beijing's practice of assigning Chinese names to places in Arunachal Pradesh, calling the move "vain and preposterous".India has maintained that such actions do not alter the "undeniable" fact that Arunachal Pradesh "was, is, and will" remain an integral part of the country.Several of the locations newly marked on the official map hold strategic importance because of their proximity to the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and their role in past India-China military confrontations.Among them is Long Ju, one of the earliest flashpoints between the two countries. Chinese troops entered the area in 1959, three years before the 1962 India-China war.The official map also includes Maja village in Upper Subansiri district near Long Ju, Bisa village and the strategically significant mountain passes of Dzo La, Riza La and Pukur La.Another key location is Thag La, the high-altitude pass where one of the opening battles of the 1962 India-China war took place.Jairampur in Changlang district has also been formally identified. The town serves as an important logistics hub for the movement of security forces towards eastern Arunachal Pradesh and the Myanmar border.Other locations added to the map include the high-altitude lake Sambho Sarovar, Bara Kundun, Chhota Kundun, Dhan Bari, Pritnagar, Teritnagar, Ramnagar, Jaswant Garh, Sagar, Padma, Jyotinagar, Baisakhi, Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, Chhota Ropuk, Bara Ropuk, Shivaji Nagar, Sunpura, Kamlang Nagar and Buddhamandir.India has repeatedly dismissed China's attempts to assign what it calls "fictitious names" to places in Arunachal Pradesh, saying such efforts seek to create "baseless narratives" and cannot alter the "undeniable" reality on the ground. New Delhi has also warned that such actions could undermine efforts to improve bilateral ties.China first issued a list of six standardised names for places in what it calls Zangnan in 2017. It followed this with a second list covering 15 locations in 2021 and another naming 11 places in 2023. Beijing uses the term Zangnan to refer to Arunachal Pradesh, a claim India has consistently rejected.
Article Summary: Arunachal pradesh chief minister pema khandu rejects reports of chinese military encroachment in the state. He said that the army was effectively patrolling and safeguarding the territory. His remarks came a day after the centre identified 27 locations in the border state by their standard names on the official map.

Article Text:

NEW DELHI: Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju on Saturday stepped up his attack on Congress , accusing the party of failing to acknowledge its "errors and shortcomings."In a post on X, Rijiju contrasted the current Congress leadership with former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, saying she had been "blunt" in admitting the actions she took during the Emergency.Sharing a video of Indira Gandhi, Rijiju wrote, "Although... we do not agree with the policies and the steps taken by the former Prime Minister Smt. Indira Gandhi ji, she was blunt in admitting the actions that she had taken.""Now, Congress party is not even realising their own errors & shortcomings," he added.In the video, Indira Gandhi is seen defending the arrest of former deputy prime minister Morarji Desai and other Opposition leaders, alleging that they were "destroying democracy."Rijiju's remarks came hours after Congress MP Rahul Gandhi hit back at his challenge to the party to extend "unconditional support" to the Women's Reservation Bill. Gandhi questioned the Centre's decision to link implementation of the legislation with the delimitation exercise.Reiterating the Congress' position, Rahul called for the implementation of the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, "without any conditions.""Mr Rijiju, who would know better than you, as the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs - that the Women's Reservation Bill 2023 has already been passed unanimously, with the full support of the Congress," Rahul posted on X.The question is, why has it still not been implemented even after three years, and why do you now want to unnecessarily link it to delimitation? Implement the 2023 law. Without any conditions," he added.Earlier in the day, Rijiju had challenged the Congress to support the Women's Reservation Bill unconditionally after Gandhi called for greater freedom of expression for women.The opposition has demanded that women's reservation be delinked from the delimitation exercise.The Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023, was passed by both Houses of Parliament.However, its implementation has not moved forward after the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill fell in the Lok Sabha on April 17, failing to secure the constitutionally required two-thirds majority of members present and voting.The Bill provided for 33 percent reservation for women in legislatures, along with provisions linked to delimitation of Lok Sabha constituencies.

NEW DELHI: Congress Rajya Sabha member Pawan Khera on Saturday attacked the PM Modi-led Centre over a US Senate bill proposing tougher sanctions on countries buying Russian oil, questioning whether India is truly free to make its own decisions.Speaking to news agency ANI in Prayagraj, Khera alleged India was being pressured by other countries over its purchases of Russian oil.He said, "Does it look like India is truly independent? Anyone who comes blackmails India; anyone who comes along dictates terms, saying you can buy oil from here, you can buy this much, you cannot buy that much. Demand answers from those who go around the country calling themselves 'Vishwaguru' but lack the courage to even enter Parliament. Article Title: ‘Honey-trapped’ IAF officer held for allegedly sharing classified defence data

NEW DELHI: An Indian Air Force (IAF) Wing Commander has been arrested for allegedly leaking sensitive defence information after being honey-trapped through social media by Pakistani intelligence operatives, officials said.According to an ANI report, the officer was under surveillance by the IAF intelligence wing before he was arrested and handed over to law enforcement agencies. Due to proactive measures, he was caught. The IAF has zero tolerance for such activities."Sources said the officer allegedly fell victim to a honey trap operated by Pakistani intelligence personnel through social media. He is also accused of installing data-stealing software on a colleague's mobile phone in an alleged attempt to gain access to the device.The arrest followed specific inputs shared by the IAF intelligence wing with the Delhi Police, sources said.Further investigation into the case is underway.The incident comes amid continued concerns over attempts by Pakistani intelligence operatives to target Indian personnel and civilians through social media-based honey traps.Last year, Rajasthan Police arrested an Alwar resident, identified as Mangat Singh, for allegedly spying for Pakistan's intelligence agency ISI. Police said a surveillance operation had been launched in the state following Operation Sindoor, during which Singh's activities in the cantonment area of Alwar were found to be suspicious.According to police, Singh had allegedly been honey-trapped by a female Pakistani handler using the pseudonym Isha Sharma. NEW DELHI: Aam Aadmi Party supremo Arvind Kejriwal on Friday launched a sharp attack on the Centre over its newly introduced social media law, alleging that it is aimed at silencing criticism of the government and reflects Prime Minister Narendra Modi's growing fear of public protests.Addressing supporters, former Delhi CM Kejriwal claimed the new law would require social media platforms to take down any post flagged by the government within three hours."The Modi government has introduced a new law. If the government asks any social media platform, whether Instagram, Facebook or any other platform, to delete a post or video, it will have to be removed within three hours," he said.He alleged that the provision would be used to target posts critical of the government on issues such as paper leaks, the ethanol policy and corruption, while allowing abusive content from its supporters to remain online."If you speak against Modi ji, the government, paper leaks, the ethanol issue or corruption, your post will be deleted within three hours. But if people associated with them use abusive language or target women, no action is taken against such content," he alleged.AAP chief Kejriwal further claimed that Prime Minister Modi has become increasingly anxious after recent youth-led protests and demonstrations at Jantar Mantar."Modi ji fears the people of this country. He fears the youth, children and women. Ever since the protests at Jantar Mantar, he has been gripped by fear," Kejriwal alleged.Arguing that censorship cannot substitute governance, the former Delhi chief minister said silencing criticism would only deepen public resentment."The solution is not to silence people's voices. If the government does good work, people will praise it on their own. The public has no personal enmity with anyone. But if you suppress criticism instead of addressing people's concerns, public anger will only grow," he said.Kejriwal also warned that governments that fear their own citizens eventually lose public support."The days of a ruler who fears his own people are numbered. The more you try to suppress the voices of the people, the stronger their anger will become," he said.Earlier to this, Kejriwal also claimed that Meta restricted his account and slammed Mark Zuckerberg-led social media giant.

Article Title: China planted trees the Taklamakan Desert for nearly 50 years. Satellites now show the landscape is capturing more carbon than it releases
Article Text:
China's shelterbelt initiative has made remarkable strides, turning arid desert borders into thriving carbon sinks. Through strategic vegetation choices, this project now captures more carbon dioxide than it expels. This achievement is anchored in mountain meltwater, vital for its irrigation systems. The initiative showcases the powerful impact of ecological restoration given optimal environmental conditions, though future water supply will be critical for sustaining these achievements.

How China built a green barrier around the Taklamakan

Satellites revealed the desert was quietly absorbing carbon

Mountain meltwater made the project possible

Why tree planting does not always succeed

The science behind the Taklamakan's changing climate

What the Taklamakan Desert project really shows

For decades, the Taklamakan Desert has stood as one of the harshest landscapes in Asia. Stretching across China's Xinjiang region, it is defined by vast sand dunes, sparse rainfall and conditions that leave little room for plant life. Yet the edges of this immense desert have been changing slowly, almost quietly. Rows of shelter forests, shrubs and restored vegetation have gradually spread across areas once dominated by bare sand. What began as an ambitious effort to slow desert expansion has developed into something with wider environmental significance.Recent satellite observations now suggest that parts of this restored landscape are removing more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere than they release, offering a rare example of large-scale desert-edge afforestation producing measurable climate benefits under very specific conditions. Ultimately, the Taklamakan's transformation stands as a cautious success story rather than a universal blueprint, one that underscores how ecological restoration depends less on ambition alone and more on the specific natural resources a landscape happens to provide.As reported by the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, China began its Three-North Shelterbelt Programme in 1978 to tackle growing desertification across the country's northern regions.Often referred to as the "Great Green Wall", the project stretches across several provinces and aims to reduce wind erosion, stabilise shifting sands and protect farmland and settlements from advancing deserts.The Taklamakan became one of the programme's most challenging frontiers. Rather than attempting to fill the desert itself with forests, planners concentrated on its margins, where carefully selected vegetation could survive with irrigation and provide a protective barrier against blowing sand.Over many years, this strategy expanded into an extensive network of planted trees, shrubs and shelterbelts surrounding sections of the desert.According to the study published in PNAS, titled ‘ Human-induced biospheric carbon sink: Impact from the Taklamakan Afforestation Project ’ reveals that the latest evidence comes from observations made using Solar-Induced Fluorescence, or SIF. During photosynthesis, plants release a faint signal in the near-infrared part of the spectrum. It cannot be seen by the human eye, but satellites are capable of detecting it from space.By tracking this fluorescence over time, scientists can estimate how actively vegetation is absorbing carbon dioxide. Instead of relying solely on ground measurements, the approach provides a broad picture across remote landscapes where regular field monitoring would be difficult.The observations showed persistent photosynthetic activity around the restored areas bordering the Taklamakan. That activity indicates the vegetation is functioning as a carbon sink, storing more carbon than it emits under present conditions.Scientists involved in the research stress that the effect should not be compared with dense tropical forests. Plant cover around the desert remains relatively sparse, resembling dry shrubland rather than continuous woodland. Even so, detecting consistent carbon uptake in such an arid environment is considered an important finding.The success of the project depends far less on the trees themselves than on the landscape surrounding the desert. The Taklamakan is enclosed by several major mountain ranges, including the Kunlun, Pamir and Tian Shan mountains. Snow and glaciers in these high elevations feed rivers flowing into the Tarim Basin. Meltwater supports irrigation systems that allow planted vegetation to survive despite the desert's extremely dry climate.Without that water supply, maintaining large-scale planting would be far more difficult. In dry environments, water usually determines whether vegetation expands or disappears, regardless of planting efforts.This also explains why the findings cannot easily be applied elsewhere. Similar projects in deserts without reliable mountain runoff would require alternative water sources, whether through desalination or groundwater extraction, both of which bring environmental and economic limitations.Large afforestation projects often receive attention as climate solutions, yet they have produced mixed outcomes around the world.Northern China's earlier planting campaigns have attracted criticism because many trees struggled to survive in arid regions. Species with high water demands sometimes depleted underground reserves, placing additional pressure on already scarce resources. Where vegetation failed, exposed soils could once again become vulnerable to erosion.The Taklamakan project appears to have avoided some of those problems by combining irrigation, suitable planting locations and gradual expansion rather than attempting to establish forests across the desert itself.Even so, long-term success remains closely linked to future water supplies. The rivers supporting these shelterbelts are partly sustained by glaciers, and those glaciers are shrinking as temperatures continue to rise. Increased meltwater may temporarily support vegetation, but over time the available supply could decline as ice reserves diminish.Planting vegetation will impact more than just the amount of carbon sequestered. Vegetation also changes the interactions that take place between the Earth's surface and sunlight.Desert sands in an unbroken state are highly reflective. Trees and bushes, however, are much darker, and thus reflect less sunlight back into space. This is called a lower albedo effect, which has led some scientists studying the climate question whether large-scale desert greening might lead to warming.On the other hand, vegetation does play an important role in the process of evaporation-transpiration. Through this process, water is emitted into the atmosphere, leading to a cooling effect. It is possible that the presence of vegetation could even lead to more precipitation due to higher humidity levels.Present data in the Taklamakan shows that the current cooling effect of plants outweighs the warming effect due to their presence in the area.The Taklamakan project does not suggest deserts can simply be transformed into forests or that tree planting alone can offset global greenhouse gas emissions.Instead, it demonstrates that carefully planned ecological restoration can work under favourable environmental conditions. Geography, water availability and long-term management all appear to have been essential ingredients behind the outcome.The study also highlights the importance of measuring restoration projects rather than assuming they succeed. Satellite observations now allow scientists to monitor carbon uptake across vast landscapes, providing evidence that was difficult to obtain only a few years ago.For now, the vegetation surrounding the Taklamakan offers an example of how degraded land can regain ecological function when natural resources, engineering and sustained management align. Whether those gains endure over the coming decades will depend largely on the future of the water systems that made them possible in the first place.
Article Summary: China's shelterbelt initiative has turned arid desert borders into thriving carbon sinks. Through strategic vegetation choices, this project now captures more carbon dioxide than it expels. This achievement is anchored in mountain meltwater, vital for its irrigation systems.

Article Title: FIFA president Gianni Infantino denies alleged affair, calls UEFA payoff claims 'defamatory'
Article Text:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez, File)

Infantino, through a FIFA spokesperson, dismissed the claims as false and defamatory.

What the report alleges

UEFA responds

Fresh Controversy Adds to Pressure on Infantino

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has strongly denied allegations that UEFA funds were used to finance a severance package for a former employee with whom he allegedly had a relationship during his time as UEFA general secretary.The allegations, published in an investigation by The Daily Telegraph, claim the woman received a rapid promotion, a significant salary increase and, after leaving UEFA, a six-figure exit package that allegedly included funding for a business school MBA."FIFA president Gianni Infantino strongly denies these allegations, and they are categorically untrue. Any insinuation of inappropriate conduct or violation of statutes or regulations is defamatory."The spokesperson also stressed that neither UEFA nor FIFA had ever received a complaint regarding Infantino's conduct."No employee at UEFA and FIFA has ever raised a complaint regarding Mr Infantino's behaviour because there never was an incident where he was involved," a FIFA spokesman told the publication.According to The Daily Telegraph, the alleged events took place while Infantino served as UEFA general secretary between 2009 and 2016.The report claims the woman, initially employed in a junior administrative role, was quickly promoted to a managerial position with a salary of around 160,000 Swiss francs.It further alleges that then-UEFA president Michel Platini became aware of the relationship and gave Infantino an ultimatum, after which the employee left the organisation. The investigation also alleges that UEFA paid the woman a six-figure departure package and covered MBA tuition fees worth approximately £45,000 per year, with the payments allegedly coming from funds earmarked for grassroots football development.UEFA has reportedly confirmed that a departure payment was made to the individual in question but said the payment was made in accordance with the rules that were applicable at the time. The governing body also said the payment covered fees for the woman to complete an MBA course at a local business school.UEFA added that its regulations have since been strengthened and now reflect the standards expected of a modern international sporting organisation.The allegations come at a difficult time for Gianni Infantino, who is already facing scrutiny over his leadership of FIFA after the governing body withdrew a controversial private investment proposal linked to the commercial future of the World Cup. The plan sparked criticism from several football associations over concerns about transparency and governance, prompting Infantino to apologise to FIFA's 211 member associations.
Article Summary: Gianni infantino has strongly denied allegations that uefa funds were used to finance a severance package for a former employee with whom he allegedly had a relationship. The allegations, published in an investigation by the daily telegraph, claim the woman received a rapid promotion, a significant salary increase and, after leaving uefa, a six-figure exit package that allegedly included funding for a business school mba.

Article Title: 'Internal matter for us': MEA dismisses US lawmaker's criticism of FCRA Bill
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Friday rejected criticism of India's foreign funding law, saying the issue is an internal matter on which Parliament will take a decision.During a bi-weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said several countries, including the United States, regulate foreign funds and foreign financing."Regarding the issue you are referring to, we have seen it, and several comments have been made on it. As far as legislative matters are concerned, and particularly matters relating to India's own legislation, this is an internal matter for us, on which our Parliament takes the decision," Jaiswal said."I would also like to tell you that there are several countries in the world, including the United States, that regulate foreign funds and foreign financing," he added.The remarks came days after a US lawmaker criticised the proposed amendments to India's foreign funding law, alleging they could allow the government to take over churches and religious charities and warning that the issue could affect India-US ties.Also read: Monsoon Session: Congress issues whip to MPs ahead of FCRA Bill discussion in Parliament US Congressman Riley Moore said the proposed changes to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act (FCRA) amounted to "a clear attack against Christians" and urged India not to proceed with the legislation in its current form.In a post on X, the Republican Congressman from West Virginia said Christianity had a long history in India dating back to the arrival of St Thomas the Apostle on the Malabar Coast."But despite this long Christian history, India's Parliament is considering amending the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act to permit government takeovers of churches and religious charities," Moore wrote."This is a clear attack against Christians. If this bill proceeds in this way, it would be a point of major concern in our bilateral relationship with India," he added.The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 proposes the creation of a Designated Authority to take over the management of foreign contributions and assets created using such funds if an organisation's FCRA registration is cancelled, surrendered or lapses after not being renewed.The Bill specifies that where such assets include a place of worship, the Designated Authority must ensure its religious character is preserved.It also proposes reducing the maximum punishment for violations of the Act from five years' imprisonment to one year.The FCRA regulates the receipt and utilisation of foreign contributions by NGOs, charitable trusts, educational institutions, religious bodies and other associations. According to the Ministry of Home Affairs, 13,520 organisations received foreign contributions worth Rs 55,741 crore between 2019 and 2022.Government data shows that as of July 15, 2026, there were 14,449 active FCRA registrations, while 22,498 had been cancelled and another 15,212 had expired.
Article Summary: Mea spokesperson randhir jaiswal said several countries, including the united states, regulate foreign funds and foreign financing. Comments come days after a us lawmaker criticised the proposed amendments to india's foreign funding law. Us congressman riley moore said the proposed changes amounted to "a clear attack against christians"

Article Title: India’s first satellite-guided chopper approached launched at HAL airport
Article Text:

BENGALURU: HAL Airport in Bengaluru has become the first airport in India to operationalise a satellite-guided helicopter approach procedure, a move expected to improve safety, reduce flight times and enable more reliable all-weather operations.“The Required Navigation Performance Category H (RNP CAT H) approach, developed by the Airports Authority of India (AAI), is designed exclusively for helicopters. The procedure was validated through flight trials by HAL test pilots and approved by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA),” HAL said Friday.The new approach, it added, enables helicopters to fly highly accurate, optimised flight paths using satellite-based navigation, allowing them to safely negotiate terrain and urban obstacles while operating in adverse weather conditions.According to HAL, the procedure cuts the approach time to HAL Airport from around 12 minutes to about 4 minutes.“The operationalisation of India’s first RNP CAT H helicopter approach is a significant milestone for the country’s aviation ecosystem. This capability enhances the safety, efficiency and accessibility of helicopter operations and establishes a benchmark for similar procedures to be implemented at airports across the country,” HAL chairman and managing director Ravi K said.Besides improving safety, the system is expected to enhance operational efficiency and airspace capacity by allowing smoother integration of helicopter and fixed-wing aircraft movements. It also reduces the noise footprint over urban areas by enabling more precise flight paths.The faster approach routes are expected to benefit time-critical operations such as air ambulance services and search-and-rescue missions. HAL Airport, which handles nearly 50 helicopter movements every day, is one of the country’s busiest helicopter hubs. The introduction of the RNP CAT H procedure addresses a long-standing gap in India’s aviation infrastructure and could serve as a model for similar helicopter navigation procedures at other airports.
Article Summary: Hal airport in bengaluru has become the first airport in india to operationalise a satellite-guided helicopter approach procedure. The move is expected to improve safety, reduce flight times and enable more reliable all-weather operations. Hal airport, which handles nearly 50 helicopter movements every day, is one of the country's busiest helicopter hubs.
